one_liner: Zig-to-WebAssembly Apple ProRes decoder for JavaScript runtimes; about 2.3-2.8x native FFmpeg 7.1.1 throughput on an Apple M4.
what_it_does: TurboRes decodes Apple ProRes packets (422 Proxy/LT/Standard/HQ, 4444 and 4444 XQ, 10- and 12-bit, alpha, interlaced) to planar YUV in browsers, Node, Deno and Bun. You get ProRes in the browser without WebCodecs hardware support or ffmpeg.wasm. The API is its own, not FFmpeg's: `await Decoder.create({ proresFourCc, useSharedMemory, concurrency, allowedOutputFormats })`, then `decoder.decode(packetBytes, frame)` per packet. Errors come back as values, the output frame is a view into wasm memory, and demuxing is left to the caller (for example Mediabunny).
how_it_is_fast: The decoder is written from scratch in Zig and compiled to wasm32 with SIMD128, threads and bulk memory (ReleaseSmall). Entropy decoding is nearly branchless, uses a LUT, reads bits through a 64-bit accumulator, and decodes slice pairs interleaved for instruction-level parallelism. The 8x8 IDCT is a float AAN (Arai-Agui-Nakajima) transform with dequantization, AAN scale factors and bit-depth scaling folded into one multiply. The transpose, the float-to-u16 conversion and the 128-bit stores are vectorized, and pixel-format conversion is fused into the store. Shared-memory threading splits every frame across workers dynamically, with no allocation after the first packet.
when_to_use: Decoding ProRes in a web app (editor, preview or transcoder front end) where WebCodecs has no ProRes support and ffmpeg.wasm is too slow: the README table gives 2.6-3.4x ffmpeg.wasm throughput on the same machine (derived from page data).
High-resolution ProRes 422 HQ or 4444 at faster than real time on CPU only: 250 FPS at 4K with shared-memory threads on an M4 MacBook Air.
Pipelines that already demux with Mediabunny or similar and need planar 8/10/12-bit output (I420/I422/I444, with or without alpha) without a separate conversion pass.
Node, Deno or Bun servers that want a ProRes decoder without native FFmpeg binaries or N-API builds.
when_not_to_use: You need encoding or any codec other than ProRes: it is decode-only and ProRes-only.

You need output bit-identical to FFmpeg or Apple's decoder: PR #3 measured Y/U/V only 84-87% bit-identical to FFmpeg 6.0 (max difference 2) and 97.2-97.7% to VideoToolbox, despite the README's 'bit-exact' claim.
Native x86-64 apps that can link FFmpeg: FFmpeg's ProRes IDCT has x86 SIMD but none on aarch64, so the 2-3x lead measured on an M4 versus scalar C may shrink on x86. There are no x86 numbers.
Pages that cannot be cross-origin isolated (COOP/COEP): you lose shared-memory threading and fall back to the slower worker-pool mode or single-threaded decoding.
Risk-averse production use: the first release was 2026-06-29, the project has one main author, and a 4x 4444 output-scale bug shipped until 1.2.2.

integration.form: npm module (ESM and UMD builds with an inlined wasm binary and inlined worker)
integration.dependencies: none at runtime (zero npm dependencies; the wasm is built with Zig 0.16 for development)
integration.min_toolchain: Runtime with WebAssembly SIMD128, threads and Atomics.waitAsync for shared-memory mode; building needs Zig 0.16 and Node/npm
integration.platforms: Any JavaScript runtime with wasm SIMD128 (Chromium, Firefox and Safari per the README; Node, Deno, Bun); shared-memory threading needs cross-origin isolation in browsers
integration.thread_safety: Each Decoder serializes its own packets with an internal mutex and resolves results in queue order. Within a packet, work is split across shared-memory workers. A Frame is locked while in flight (FrameLockedError).

gotchas: The decoder trusts the caller-supplied FourCC for bit depth. The benchmark hard-codes 'apch', so its '4444 @ 1080p' row decodes the 4444 file to 10-bit, while FFmpeg outputs yuva444p12le. In ap4h/ap4x mode, every 4444 output was 4x too small until PR #3 (fixed in 1.2.2, 2026-07-09), and the bug went unnoticed because the test's reference file had been generated by TurboRes itself.

Test oracle: tests/tests.test.ts compares frames against gzipped framedata files produced by TurboRes, not by FFmpeg or Apple, so the suite catches regressions but not conformance. The IDCT ends with a truncating float-to-u32 conversion clamped to [0, 2^depth-1], while FFmpeg clamps to [4, 2^depth-5]; together these account for the 1-2 LSB differences.

Harness asymmetries behind the table: TurboRes pre-demuxes every packet into memory and runs 3 warm-up passes. The native FFmpeg script times CLI demux plus decode as (11-loop minus 1-loop rtime)/10. benchmark-ffmpeg-wasm.html runs stream_loop 0 and 9 (1 and 10 passes, not 1 and 11) with 10 threads hard-coded and leaves the arithmetic to the reader. No single-threaded configuration of TurboRes or ffmpeg.wasm is committed, and neither the browser nor the native thread count is named.

To reproduce, build the wasm with ./scripts/build-zig.sh --release first. benchmark-turbores.html imports ../src/index, which inlines build/lib.wasm, and the default build (also run by npm test) is Debug. Release builds use ReleaseSmall, not ReleaseFast.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick TurboRes when the media is ProRes; the catalogued wasm video siblings target other codecs (Pare encodes H.264 and beats ffmpeg.wasm's assembly-less x264, WXInlinePlayer plays H.264/H.265). For a general-purpose multi-codec decoder in the browser, ffmpeg.wasm is still the fallback.
verified_claims_summary: Author-run table (TurboRes 1.2.0 versus FFmpeg 7.1.1 CLI, ffmpeg.wasm 0.11 and VideoToolbox on an Apple M4 10-core MacBook Air, averaged over 10 file decodes). Single-threaded: 42 vs 15 FPS at 422 HQ 4K and 450 vs 161 at 422 Proxy 1080p (2.3-2.8x, derived from page data). Multithreaded: 250 vs 107 FPS at 4K and 2310 vs 948 at Proxy (2.2-2.5x across the four files, derived from page data), plus 250 vs 160 against hardware-accelerated FFmpeg. The native baseline runs FFmpeg's scalar C ProRes IDCT on aarch64, and the browser running the wasm is not named.
status_note: Active but very young (npm 1.0.0 on 2026-06-29, 1.2.2 on 2026-07-09, last commit 2026-07-14). MPL-2.0 (file-level copyleft), zero runtime dependencies, about 50 kB gzipped, so it is easy to adopt. Draft PR #5 ('TurboRes native') adds native x86-64 and aarch64 builds with M4 and x86-64 benchmarks and is worth rechecking for an x86 comparison against FFmpeg's SIMD IDCT. No harness flaw invalidates the numbers, but the 'bit-exact' claim is false against FFmpeg (max difference 2) and the tests are self-referential.
